{"memo": "Executive Summary — oniguruma-parser Library Selection

Introduction: oniguruma-parser is a TypeScript toolkit for parsing, validating, traversing, transforming, and optimizing Oniguruma regular expressions, the engine that powers Ruby, PHP, TextMate grammars, VS Code, and Shiki. It is battle-tested through Oniguruma-To-ES and tm-grammars, which have processed tens of thousands of real-world Oniguruma patterns, demonstrating production maturity.

Contents: The README provides a table of contents linking to installation, pattern-to-AST conversion, traversal, generation, optimization, differences, and version information. It enables quick navigation for evaluators and previews the full scope of the documentation.

Install and Use: The library installs via npm install oniguruma-parser and supports ESM via import of toOnigurumaAst, CommonJS via a third-party wrapper, and direct browser use via CDN bundle. It also exposes modular Parser, Traverser, Generator, and Optimizer modules for focused use.

Convert a Pattern to an AST: Calling toOnigurumaAst with a pattern plus optional flags and compile-time options returns a detailed Oniguruma AST, and it throws when the pattern or flags are invalid. The function wraps the parser module's parse routine while automatically supplying Unicode property validation data.

Traverse and Transform an AST: This section defers all details and examples for walking and modifying the AST to the dedicated traverser module README. It contains no inline API and serves only as a pointer to that documentation.

Convert an AST to a Pattern: This section defers all details and examples for converting an AST back to pattern and flags strings to the generator module README. It contains no inline conversion logic and serves only as a pointer to that module documentation.

Optimize Regexes: The library includes a rare regex optimizer that minifies patterns and improves performance and readability while guaranteeing identical match behavior, illustrated by collapsing a verbose extended pattern into a compact equivalent. Full details are in the optimizer module README, with an interactive demo available online.

Known Differences: Known gaps are limited to rarely used features such as exotic escapes, code point sequences, absence edge cases, conditionals, callouts and certain backreferences and flags, yet more than 99.99% of about 55k real-world TextMate regexes are supported. Intentional behavior differences include limiting unenclosed backreferences to three digits and throwing errors instead of reproducing Oniguruma bugs for nested absence functions, bare escapes, and invalid standalone encoded bytes.

Oniguruma Version: All releases to date follow Oniguruma 6.9.10 from early 2025 with Unicode 16.0.0, and syntax changes since 6.0.0 have remained backward compatible apart from new additions and edge-case fixes. Version 6.9.8 remains the practical baseline for JavaScript projects through vscode-oniguruma, VS Code, and Shiki, but its syntax differences from 6.9.10 are minor and non-blocking.

{"memo": "CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow definitions for CSS generated from MDN data for autocompletion and type checking. Further examples show invalid properties and values producing type errors.

Table of Contents lists links to all major documentation sections including Style, At-rule, and Pseudo types. It serves as navigation for Generics, Usage, troubleshooting, version history, and contributing.

Getting Started: Install the package with npm install csstype. Then import its TypeScript or Flow types to get autocompletion and type checking for CSS properties and values.

Style Types: CSS Properties are grouped into All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, and Svg categories with Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (array values), and HyphenFallback variants, e.g., Properties, PropertiesHyphen, PropertiesFallback.

At-Rule Types: This section documents typed descriptors for counter-style, font-face, and viewport rules in Default, Hyphen, Fallback, and HyphenFallback variants. In TypeScript they live under the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use the AtRule prefix with dollar sign.

Pseudo Types: This section defines string literal types for pseudo classes and elements through the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos requiring arguments and SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics: All interfaces accept optional Length and Time generics defaulting to string or zero and string to model unitless zero and time values. You can override them for example with string or number to allow numeric lengths or times for specific platforms and libraries.

Usage: This section shows practical TypeScript examples using basic properties, fallback arrays for CSS in JS libraries, pseudo mappings, and hyphen cased variants via interface extension. It also demonstrates assigning typed style objects to button element style with Object assign.

What Should I Do When I Get Type Errors?: This section explains that type errors can stem from rejected specs, TypeScript literal widening, or evolving CSS and vendor specs, and advises checking existing issues. It then shows how to work around them locally with module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2, so conflicts can occur if both major versions are installed. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer line through the overrides field in package json for npm.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes shared data types for reuse in user code. In TypeScript they are accessed through the DataType namespace and in Flow through the DataType prefix with dollar sign.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 moves all property and at-rule types into namespaces and withholds data types due to instability. It also introduces improved autocompletion hacks, a new Time generic, and Flow Strict exact type improvements.

Contributing: This section warns never to edit generated index files directly and requires setting a specific git merge driver to true to avoid rebase conflicts. It also lists npm scripts for building, watching, testing, and checking code.

Commands: The Commands subsection lists npm scripts for the development workflow. Build generates and checks typings, watch rebuilds on save, test runs tests, and lazy checks lints and formats everything.

Recommendation: Adopt csstype for MDN-based autocompletion and type-safe styles, using Fallback variants for CSS-in-JS, Length/Time generics for platform needs, and documented augmentation or assertion workarounds while staying on the v3 line.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled Worker 1 Style summary and Worker 2 summaries in README document order, one paragraph per section plus closing recommendation, preserving original wording without adding new facts."}

Table of content provides a linked list of all main documentation topics in the README. It allows readers to quickly navigate to type definitions, usage guidance, version history, and contribution notes.

Style types: Properties are categorized as All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, Svg with Standard/Vendor split into longhand/shorthand. Variations include Default camelCase, Hyphen kebab-case, Fallback array values, and HyphenFallback combination.

Pseudo types defines string literal types for pseudo classes and elements under the Pseudos type. It distinguishes AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos that need arguments from SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics explains the two optional generics for length and time that default to string or zero and string. It shows how to override them to allow numeric values for platforms that interpret numbers with a specific unit.

Usage demonstrates practical patterns such as basic style objects, fallback value arrays, pseudo selector maps, hyphen-cased properties, and assigning styles to an HTMLElement. It emphasizes using PropertiesFallback for CSS-in-JS fallbacks and extending Properties with PropertiesHyphen to support both casings.

What should I do when I get type errors? guides users to verify correct usage, check existing issues, and work around problems caused by custom properties or evolving specifications. It recommends module augmentation as the preferred TypeScript fix and type assertion as an alternative, with type assertion guidance for Flow.

Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may arise when both major versions are installed together. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer release through the overrides field in the package configuration file.

Version 3.1 exposes CSS data types through the DataType namespace in TypeScript and the corresponding prefix in Flow. It makes reusable value types directly available to consumers.

Version 3.0 moves property types and at-rule types into dedicated namespaces and stops exposing raw data types that could be renamed or removed. It also adds a string-and-object hack for better autocompletion, a new generic for time values, and improved Flow support with strict and exact types.

Contributing warns that generated declaration files must never be edited directly and requires enabling a specific git merge driver after cloning to avoid conflicts. It stresses that all typings changes come from generation so history of generated output remains traceable.

Commands lists npm scripts for building and type checking typings, watching for changes, running tests, and performing a combined lazy check with lint and format. These commands support the generation workflow described in the contributing guidelines.

Recommendation: Adopt csstype for type-safe CSS-in-JS using PropertiesFallback with hyphen support, leverage length/time generics and namespaced at-rule, pseudo, and data types, follow the type-error and version-migration guidance, and contribute only via the generation workflow.","concerns":[],"rationale":"Assembled Worker 2 summaries in listed document order, inserted Worker 1 Style types summary between Table of content and At-rule types, kept one paragraph per section, and added closing recommendation."}

Table of content: The table of content lists links to all major sections including style types, at-rule types, pseudo types, generics, usage, error handling, version history and contributing. It enables quick navigation to the relevant documentation without reading the whole file.

Style types: CSSType groups properties into All, Standard (with Longhand/Shorthand subcategories), Vendor, Obsolete, and Svg categories. Each offers Default camelCase, Hyphen kebab-case, Fallback array-value, and HyphenFallback variants like PropertiesHyphenFallback.

At-rule types: At-rule types provide typed interfaces with descriptors for counter-style, font-face and viewport in Default, Hyphen, Fallback and HyphenFallback variations. In TypeScript they are accessed through the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use the AtRule prefix with dollar sign naming.

Pseudo types: Pseudo types provide string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements through the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos that require an argument and SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics: All property interfaces accept two optional generics for length and time that default to string or zero and string to reflect CSS rules for unitless zero. These generics can be customized for platforms that accept numeric lengths and times with a specific unit.

Usage: Usage shows importing CSS types and assigning plain style objects, using PropertiesFallback to allow array fallback values and using SimplePseudos as keys for hover styles. It also demonstrates combining camelCase and kebab-case through interface extension and applying typed styles to button elements.

What should I do when I get type errors?: This section explains that type errors can stem from custom properties, evolving specifications, vendor implementations and TypeScript type widening and advises checking existing issues and filing new ones. It then shows local fixes through module augmentation and type assertion in TypeScript and through type assertion in Flow with examples for missing properties and custom properties.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may occur if both major versions are installed together. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer major version through npm overrides in package json.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes data types for reuse in user code. These are accessed as DataType Color in TypeScript and with dollar sign naming in Flow.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 introduces namespaced property and at-rule types while withdrawing direct exposure of data types that may be renamed or removed. It also adds the string and number intersection hack for autocompletion with PropertyValue unpacking, a new generic for time and Flow strict and exact-type improvements.

Contributing: Contributing warns never to edit the generated definition files directly and requires setting the git merge ours driver after forking to avoid rebase conflicts. It directs contributors to the build, watch, test and lazy scripts for generating, checking and formatting the typings.

Commands: Commands lists four npm scripts for the development workflow. Build generates and type-checks typings, watch rebuilds on save, test runs tests and lazy type-checks lints and formats everything.

Recommendation: We recommend adopting csstype for TypeScript and Flow CSS-in-JS work for its comprehensive MDN-based type safety, flexible Style, At-rule, Pseudo, Fallback and Generics coverage, and clear error-handling and upgrade paths, provided projects pin to Version 3.x with npm overrides to avoid v2 conflicts.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in document order inferred from Worker 2 sequence and Table of content listing, inserting Worker 1 Style types paragraph between Table of content and At-rule types, preserving all keywords verbatim and adding closing recommendation per brief."}

Pseudo Types: Pseudo types offer string literals for pseudo classes and elements through the Pseudos type, which extends SimplePseudos for single-variation selectors like hover and AdvancedPseudos for function-like selectors like not that require arguments.

Generics: All property interfaces accept optional generics for length defaulting to string or zero and time defaulting to string, which can be customized to numeric types so platforms that accept numbers with implicit units are correctly typed.

Examples show invalid properties like colour and invalid values like textAlign middle producing type errors in both languages.

Getting started: Installation is done with npm install csstype. After installing, the types can be imported for immediate type-checked styling.

Table of content: This section lists links to all major sections including Style types, At-rule types, Pseudo types, Generics, Usage, error handling, versions, and contributing. It serves as navigation aid rather than substantive content.

Style types: Style types offer CSS property interfaces in five categories — All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, Svg — and four variations: Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (allows string|string[] arrays), and HyphenFallback. Standard and Vendor further split into Longhand and Shorthand subcategories.

At-rule types: At-rule interfaces describe descriptors for @counter-style, @font-face, and @viewport, each offered in Default, Hyphen, Fallback, and HyphenFallback variations. In TypeScript they live under the AtRule namespace such as AtRule.Viewport while in Flow they use the AtRule$ prefix such as AtRule$Viewport.

Pseudo types: Pseudos provides string literals for pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements and extends two subcategories. AdvancedPseudos covers function-like pseudos such as :not without parentheses, while SimplePseudos covers plain single-variation pseudos such as :hover.

Generics: All interfaces accept two optional generics for length and time, defaulting to TLength = string | 0 where zero needs no unit and TTime = string. They can be overridden, for example to string | number, to allow numeric lengths like width 100 and numeric times like transitionDuration 1000 on platforms with implicit units.

Usage: Basic usage imports CSS.Properties for plain style objects, while CSS.PropertiesFallback allows array values for fallback declarations like display with -webkit-flex and flex. Additional patterns include mapping SimplePseudos to properties, extending Properties with PropertiesHyphen to support kebab-case, and assigning typed objects to HTMLElement.style via Object.assign.

What should I do when I get type errors?: Type errors can arise from correct code due to CSS Custom Properties, frequently changing specs, vendor-specific implementations, rejected specs, or TypeScript literal widening, so users should first verify correctness and search existing issues before filing a new one. If unresolved, the guide recommends local fixes via module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow, with examples for missing properties and custom properties.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2, so installing ^3.2.0 alongside ^2.0.0 may cause conflicts. For npm, the documented fix is to force resolution with an overrides entry for csstype ^3.2.0 in package.json.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes data types as DataType.Color in TypeScript and DataType$Color in Flow. This allows consumers to directly reuse low-level value types in their own typings.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 moves all property types under the Property namespace and all at-rules under the AtRule namespace, while withdrawing direct exposure of data types like Color that may be renamed or removed. It also introduces the string-and-empty autocompletion hack with PropertyValue unwrapping, a new time generic, and Flow Strict with exact types.

Contributing: Generated files index.d.ts and index.js.flow must never be edited directly, and contributors must run git config merge.ours.driver true after forking to prevent rebase conflicts. All typings changes originate from generator sources and are committed to make diffs reviewable.

{"memo": "CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and static checking of properties and values. Usage is illustrated with TypeScript and Flow imports where misspelled properties or invalid values produce type errors.

Getting started: Installation is done with a single npm install command for the csstype package. No further setup is required to start importing the types in a project.

Table of content: The table lists the main documentation sections to aid navigation. It links to style and rule and usage and troubleshooting and version and contribution topics.

Style types: Properties are grouped by category: All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, and Svg, with Standard/Vendor split into Longhand/Shorthand subcategories. Four variations exist: Default camelCase, Hyphen kebab-case, Fallback allowing value arrays, and HyphenFallback combining both.

At-rule types: At-rule types model descriptors for counter style and font face and viewport rules in dedicated interfaces with Default and Hyphen and Fallback variations. In TypeScript they are accessed through the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use an AtRule dollar prefix.

Pseudo types: Pseudo types provide string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements under the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function like pseudos that need arguments and SimplePseudos for plain single variation pseudos.

Generics: All interfaces accept two optional generics that control allowed length and time value types for greater flexibility. Length defaults to string or zero since zero needs no unit and time defaults to string, and both can be widened to accept numbers for platforms that handle units automatically.

Usage: Basic usage imports the types and assigns plain objects to Properties for standard checking of values like width and margin. Extended patterns support fallback arrays for CSS in JS, literal pseudo selectors, hyphen cased properties by extension, and assignment onto HTMLElement style objects.

What should I do when I get type errors?: Type errors are addressed by first verifying correct CSS usage and checking for rejected specs or widening issues, then searching existing issues and filing a new one if needed. Local fixes use module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow, including patterns for missing properties and custom properties.

Version 3.2: This release breaks compatibility with version two so both major versions cannot coexist without conflicts. The documented remedy is to force resolution to the newer major line with an overrides entry in package JSON.

Version 3.1: This release exposes shared data types for reuse across projects. TypeScript accesses them through the DataType namespace while Flow uses a DataType dollar prefix.

Version 3.0: This major release moves all property and at rule types into dedicated namespaces and withdraws direct exposure of data types that may change. It also adds a string intersection hack for better autocompletion with an unpack helper plus a new time generic and stricter exact Flow types.

Contributing: Contributions must never edit the generated definition files directly since they are produced automatically and committed for change tracking. Contributors should enable the ours merge driver after cloning and use the provided npm scripts for building and watching and testing and full validation.

Commands: The commands support generating typings with type checking and rebuilding on save. Additional scripts run tests and perform combined type checking with linting and formatting.

Recommendation: For the library selection decision, csstype is recommended as a lightweight, well-maintained source of truth for CSS in TypeScript and Flow that improves correctness and developer experience without runtime cost, subject to standardizing on major version 3 and documenting local workarounds for custom properties and version conflicts.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Inserted W1 Style types summary into W2 document-order sections to achieve full coverage, preserved each worker wording as one paragraph per section, and added closing recommendation per brief."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary: csstype — Library Selection Memo for Architecture Council

CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and type checking for properties and values. It is imported as a type namespace and flags misspelled properties or invalid values at compile time.

Getting started: Installation is done with a single npm install command for csstype. No further configuration is required to begin importing its types.

Table of content: The table of content lists the major documentation sections for style types and at-rule types and pseudo types and generics and usage and troubleshooting and version history and contributing. It serves as navigation to quickly locate reference material in the document.

Style types: Properties split into All, Standard (with Longhand/Shorthand), Vendor (Longhand/Shorthand), Obsolete, and Svg categories across Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (array values), and HyphenFallback variations (e.g., Properties, PropertiesHyphenFallback).

At-rule types: At-rule types describe descriptors for counter-style and font-face and viewport rules through naming variations for default and hyphen and fallback forms. In TypeScript they live under the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use an AtRule prefix.

Pseudo types: Pseudo types provide string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements under the Pseudos type. They distinguish AdvancedPseudos for function-like cases requiring arguments from SimplePseudos for plain single-variation cases.

Generics: All interfaces accept optional generics for length defaulting to string or zero since zero needs no unit and time defaulting to string. Callers can widen these generics to numeric types so platforms that interpret numbers with fixed units type check correctly.

Usage: Basic usage imports the namespace and assigns plain objects to Properties for standard checking of values like width and margin. Fallback arrays and hyphen-cased interfaces and pseudo-mapped objects and direct assignment to element styles extend the same pattern for broader scenarios.

What should I do when I get type errors?: When type errors appear the guide advises first verifying correct CSS usage and awareness of widening and unaccepted specs then searching or filing issues. It then shows how to fix problems locally with module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow including support for custom properties.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may occur if both are installed. The guide recommends forcing a single resolution with an npm overrides entry for csstype.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes shared CSS data types for direct reuse. These types are reachable through dedicated namespaces in both TypeScript and Flow.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 moves all property and at-rule types under dedicated namespaces while withholding unstable data types. It also introduces autocompletion helpers with unpacking utilities plus a new time generic and stricter exact Flow types.

Contributing: Contributing prohibits direct edits to generated definition files since they are produced automatically and committed for change tracking. Contributors must set the recommended git merge driver after cloning to prevent rebase conflicts.

Commands: The commands section defines npm scripts for building and watching and testing the typings. It also provides a lazy script that combines type checking with linting and formatting.

Recommendation: Recommend adoption of csstype for any TypeScript/Flow CSS-in-JS or style-object work: it is zero-runtime, install-trivial, MDN-grounded, and provides broad property, at-rule, pseudo, fallback, and generic coverage with clear troubleshooting and extensibility paths; ensure a single v3.x resolution via overrides to avoid v2 conflicts.", "concerns": ["Memo assembled solely from W1 and W2 summaries without independent read of README; fidelity depends on their accuracy"], "rationale": "Assembled W2 two-sentence summaries and W1 Style types summary in inferred document order (CSSType through Commands) as one paragraph per section plus closing adoption recommendation."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary – csstype Library Selection Memo

CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and type checking for properties and values. It is imported as a type namespace in both languages with examples shown for catching misspelled properties and invalid values.

Getting Started: Installation is done with a single package manager command to add csstype as a dependency. No further configuration is required to start importing its types in a project.

Table of Content: The table of content lists the main documentation sections for style types and at-rule types and pseudo types and generics and usage and troubleshooting and version history and contributing. It serves as navigation links to each part of the document.

Style Types: Style types offer CSS property interfaces in five categories—All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, Svg—each with four variations: Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (array values), and HyphenFallback. All combines all categories; Standard and Vendor split into Longhand/Shorthand subcategories.

At-Rule Types: At-rule types provide typed interfaces with descriptors for counter style and font face and viewport rules in matching default and hyphen and fallback variations. They are accessed through the AtRule namespace in TypeScript and through the AtRule dollar prefix in Flow.

Pseudo Types: Pseudo types supply string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements grouped under the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos that need arguments and SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics: All property interfaces accept two optional generics for length and time with length defaulting to string or zero and time defaulting to string. These generics can be widened to string or number to support platforms where numeric lengths or times imply specific units.

Usage: Usage centers on typing style objects with Properties for standard camel cased properties and using PropertiesFallback to allow arrays for fallback values in CSS in JS libraries. It also shows typing pseudo selectors with SimplePseudos and supporting kebab cased names by extending hyphen interfaces and assigning typed objects to element styles.

What Should I Do When I Get Type Errors?: Troubleshooting acknowledges that type errors can stem from user mistakes or evolving specs and vendor implementations despite aiming for perfect types. It advises verifying correctness and checking existing issues then fixing locally with module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow including support for custom properties.

Version 3.2: This release is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may occur when both major versions are installed together. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer major line through the overrides field in package dot json.

Version 3.1: This release exposes data types through the DataType namespace in TypeScript and the DataType dollar prefix in Flow. It makes reusable value types such as color directly available to consumers.

Version 3.0: This major release moves all property types and at-rule types into dedicated namespaces and stops exposing data types that could be renamed or removed. It also introduces a string and object hack for autocompletion with a helper to unpack values plus a new time generic and Flow strict and exact type improvements.

Contributing: Contributing warns never to edit generated definition files directly since they are produced automatically and committed for change tracking. It requires setting the merge driver to preserve generated files after forking and cloning.

Commands: Commands lists four npm scripts for generating and checking typings and watching for changes and running tests and linting and formatting. They cover build and watch and test and lazy workflows for contributors.

Recommendation: Recommend adoption of csstype for any TypeScript or Flow CSS-in-JS work: it provides comprehensive, MDN-based type safety with flexible handling of vendor, fallback, hyphen, pseudo, at-rule, and generic cases, straightforward installation and usage, and clear guidance for troubleshooting and version migration, with active generated-file maintenance for contributors.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in document order using W2 two-sentence summaries for all sections except Style types and W1 summary for Style types, adding only a closing synthesis recommendation per assignment."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary – csstype Library Selection Memo for Architecture Council

CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and type checking of properties and values. Its introductory examples show that misspelled properties like colour and invalid values like middle for textAlign are caught as type errors in both languages.

Getting started: Installation is done with a single command using npm install csstype. No additional setup is required before importing the types into a TypeScript or Flow project.

Table of content: The Table of content provides anchor links to eight major parts of the document from Style types through Contributing. It serves only as navigation and contains no substantive guidance itself.

Style types: Style types organizes properties by category — All, Standard (plus Longhand/Shorthand), Vendor, Obsolete, Svg — and by variation: Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (allows string|string[]), and HyphenFallback. Types like Properties combine both dimensions.

At-rule types: At-rule types provide typed interfaces with descriptors for counter-style, font-face, and viewport, accessed through the AtRule namespace in TypeScript and the AtRule dollar prefix in Flow. Each at-rule offers Default, Hyphen, Fallback, and HyphenFallback variations that mirror the property type system.

Pseudo types: Pseudos exposes string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements and extends AdvancedPseudos and SimplePseudos. AdvancedPseudos covers function-like pseudos such as :not stripped of parentheses because they have infinite variations, while SimplePseudos covers plain single-variation pseudos such as :hover.

Generics: All interfaces accept two optional generics with TLength defaulting to string or zero and TTime defaulting to string to control allowed length and time value types. Libraries that accept numeric values with implicit units can override these, for example allowing width 100 with a custom length type or transitionDuration 1000 with a custom time type.

Usage: Usage centers on importing CSS from csstype and typing style objects as Properties, with PropertiesFallback enabling array fallback values for CSS-in-JS and mapped SimplePseudos types supporting pseudo selectors. Hyphen-cased properties require extending PropertiesHyphen or PropertiesHyphenFallback, and typed objects can be applied directly to elements with Object assign on button style.

What should I do when I get type errors?: The section explains that errors can come from incorrect usage, unaccepted vendor specs, TypeScript literal widening, or the fast-changing CSS specification and advises first verifying correctness and then checking or filing a GitHub issue. It recommends local fixes through module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow, including patterns for missing properties and custom properties for theming.

Version 3.2: This release breaks compatibility with version two so installing both major versions together can cause conflicts. Npm users are advised to force a single resolution with an overrides entry pinning csstype to the newer major range.

Version 3.1: This release exposes reusable CSS data types such as Color for consumers of the library. In TypeScript they appear under the DataType namespace and in Flow under the DataType dollar prefix.

Version 3.0: This major release introduced breaking namespaced property types such as AlignContent and at-rule types such as FontFace while withholding unstable data types such as Color. It also added the string autocompletion hack with PropertyValue unwrapping, a new time generic, and Flow Strict with exact types.

Contributing: Contributors must never edit the generated entry files directly because they are auto-generated and committed for change tracking. After forking and cloning, they must run the specified git config command to prevent merge conflicts during rebases.

Commands: The Commands subsection documents four npm scripts where build generates and type-checks typings, watch rebuilds on save, test runs tests, and lazy type-checks, lints, and formats everything. These cover the full generation-to-validation workflow for contributors.

Recommendation: Recommend approval of csstype for typed CSS-in-JS and design-system work given its MDN-generated coverage, TypeScript and Flow support, flexible Standard/Vendor/Svg and Hyphen/Fallback variants, generics for lengths/times, and documented escape hatches for type errors, with attention to major-version pinning per the Version 3.2 guidance.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled one paragraph per section in document order using W2's ordered summaries for all sections except Style types and W1's summary for Style types inserted between Table of content and At-rule types, plus closing recommendation for council decision."}

{"memo":"d3-sankey: Sankey diagrams visualize directed flow between nodes in an acyclic network with width proportional to flow quantity. The introduction illustrates this with United Kingdom energy production and consumption and points to an interactive editor for experimentation.

Installing: Install via npm install d3-sankey, latest release download, or unpkg CDN; supports AMD, CommonJS, vanilla exporting d3 global.

API Reference: The API reference documents the Sankey generator and its configuration methods for computing node and link positions. It also covers alignment utilities and a horizontal link shape generator for rendering.

d3.sankey(): This constructor creates a new Sankey generator preconfigured with default settings. The resulting generator can then be customized and invoked to compute a layout.

sankey(arguments...): Invoking the generator computes node and link positions for the supplied graph arguments and returns the laid out graph. The returned graph exposes a nodes array and a links array with computed layout properties.

sankey.update(graph): This method recomputes only link vertical positions after an initial layout has been computed. It is intended for interactive repositioning where node positions have changed and link endpoints must be updated.

sankey.nodes([nodes]): This accessor gets or sets how nodes are obtained from the input graph with a default that reads the nodes property. Each node object is augmented with source and target link lists plus value and index plus depth and height plus layer and computed horizontal and vertical bounds.

sankey.links([links]): This accessor gets or sets how links are obtained from the input graph with a default that reads the links property. Each link must define source and target plus numeric value and is augmented with vertical start and end positions plus width proportional to value plus index.

sankey.linkSort([sort]): This method gets or sets the sort order for links stacked vertically within each node with automatic layout by default. A null value preserves input order while a custom comparator function can explicitly control which link appears above another.

sankey.nodeId([id]): This accessor gets or sets the function used to identify nodes so links may use simple identifiers instead of object references. The default uses numeric index while a custom accessor such as one reading a name field enables readable JSON graphs without circular references.

sankey.nodeAlign([align]): This method gets or sets the alignment function that chooses the horizontal column for each node with justification as the default. The function receives each node and total depth and must return an integer column between first and last to control left to right placement.

sankey.nodeSort([sort]): This method gets or sets the sort order for nodes stacked vertically within each column with automatic layout by default. A null value preserves input order while a custom comparator function can explicitly control which node appears above another.

sankey.nodeWidth([width]): This method gets or sets the horizontal thickness of each node rectangle with a default of twenty four pixels. Changing the width affects horizontal space occupied by nodes while link thickness remains driven by values.

sankey.nodePadding([padding]): This method gets or sets the vertical separation between nodes in the same column with a default of eight pixels. Larger padding improves readability by spacing nodes while reducing room available for link widths.

sankey.extent([extent]): This method gets or sets the rectangular bounds that constrain the entire layout with a default from origin to unit coordinates. A custom extent is specified as nested coordinate pairs for left top and right bottom to fit the diagram to available screen space.

sankey.size([size]): This method provides a convenient alias for extent when the layout should start at the origin. It accepts width and height and is equivalent to setting an extent from zero zero to the given size.

sankey.iterations([iterations]): This method gets or sets the number of relaxation iterations used to optimize vertical positions during layout with a default of six. More iterations can improve compactness and reduce crossing while increasing computation time for large graphs.

Alignments: This section groups the built in horizontal alignment strategies referenced by the node alignment setting. Each strategy maps depth and height to a column to achieve left right centered or justified arrangements.

d3.sankeyLeft(node, n): This alignment places each node at the column matching its depth from sources. It produces a left leaning diagram where nodes appear as early as possible in flow order.

d3.sankeyRight(node, n): This alignment places each node at the column derived from its distance to sinks. It produces a right leaning diagram where nodes appear as late as possible in flow order.

d3.sankeyCenter(node, n): This alignment behaves like left alignment except that source free nodes are pushed as far right as possible. It yields a centered appearance that balances early placement with consolidation of isolated origins.

d3.sankeyJustify(node, n): This default alignment behaves like left alignment except that sink free nodes are moved to the far right edge. It yields a justified appearance that stretches flows across the full width while anchoring final outputs.

d3.sankeyLinkHorizontal(): This factory returns a horizontal link shape configured with source at the right edge of the source node and target at the left edge of the target node. {"memo": "d3-sankey: Sankey diagrams visualize directed flow between nodes in an acyclic network, illustrated by a 2050 scenario of United Kingdom energy production and consumption. An interactive editor called Flow-o-Matic is referenced for hands-on exploration.

Installing: Install via npm install d3-sankey, download latest release, or load from unpkg. Supports AMD, CommonJS, and vanilla with d3 global export.

API Reference: This section documents the core generator that computes node and link positions for Sankey layouts. It defines constructors, accessors, and layout tuning methods that together produce a positioned graph.

d3.sankey(): This constructor creates a new Sankey generator with default settings. It serves as the starting point for configuring nodes, links, and layout parameters.

sankey(arguments…): This invocation computes node and link positions for the supplied arguments and returns a graph object. The resulting graph exposes positioned nodes and links arrays ready for rendering.

sankey.update: This method recomputes only the vertical link positions after an initial layout has been computed. It is intended for interactive repositioning where node positions change but the overall layout need not be rebuilt.

sankey.nodes: This accessor gets or sets how nodes are derived from the input graph, accepting either a constant array or a function. Each resulting node is enriched with link references, value, index, depth, height, layer, and horizontal and vertical coordinates.

sankey.links: This accessor gets or sets how links are derived from the input graph, accepting either a constant array or a function. Each link must define source, target, and numeric value and is enriched with vertical positions, width proportional to value, and index.

sankey.linkSort: This setting controls the vertical ordering of links within each node. By default the order is automatic, while null preserves input order and a custom comparator can enforce explicit ranking.

sankey.nodeId: This accessor defines how node identity is resolved so links can use object references, numeric indexes, or string names. Custom string identifiers are especially useful for JSON graphs that cannot contain direct references.

sankey.nodeAlign: This setting selects the horizontal alignment strategy that maps each node to a column between zero and maximum depth. The default strategy justifies the diagram while custom functions can implement alternative placements.

sankey.nodeSort: This setting controls the vertical ordering of nodes within each column. By default the order is automatic, while null preserves input order and a custom comparator can enforce explicit ranking.

sankey.nodeWidth: This setting gets or sets the horizontal thickness of each node rectangle. The default width is 24 within the layout extent.

sankey.nodePadding: This setting gets or sets the vertical separation between nodes in the same column. The default padding is 8 within the layout extent.

sankey.extent: This setting gets or sets the rectangular bounds of the layout defined by lower and upper coordinate pairs. The default extent spans from zero zero to one one.

sankey.size: This method is a convenience alias for setting extent with the minimum fixed at the origin. It accepts a size pair that becomes the maximum corner of the bounds.

sankey.iterations: This setting gets or sets the number of relaxation iterations used to optimize vertical positions during layout. The default is six iterations to balance quality and performance.

Alignments: This subsection groups the built-in horizontal placement strategies referenced by the alignment setting. It provides four alternatives that trade off compactness, centering, and edge justification.

d3.sankeyLeft: This strategy places each node at a column equal to its graph depth. It produces a left-aligned diagram where sources start at the left edge.

d3.sankeyRight: This strategy places each node according to its distance from sinks rather than sources. It produces a right-aligned diagram where many nodes shift toward the right edge.

d3.sankeyCenter: This strategy behaves like left alignment except that sourceless nodes are pushed as far right as possible. It yields a more centered appearance while preserving depth-based order.

d3.sankeyJustify: This strategy behaves like left alignment except that sinkless nodes are moved to the far right edge. It is the default alignment because it emphasizes full flow from left to right.

Links: This subsection introduces the helper for drawing the curved connections between nodes. It focuses on generating suitable path data for rendering links with width proportional to flow.

d3.sankeyLinkHorizontal(): This factory returns a horizontal link shape whose endpoints derive from node edges and link vertical offsets. For rendering, paths are typically styled without fill and given stroke widths proportional to flow value.

Recommendation: For the architecture council, d3-sankey is recommended for adoption where directed-flow visualization is required: it offers standard installation, a small configurable layout API with alignment, sorting, sizing, and iteration controls, plus a link-shape helper, enabling rapid integration without opening the full README.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled one paragraph per section in README document order using W1 Installing summary and W2 summaries for all other sections, plus closing recommendation, per orchestrator assignment."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary - magic-string Library Selection Memo

magic-string: magic-string is a small fast utility for lightly modifying strings while generating accurate source maps without full AST parsing. It is ideal when recast-like tooling is overkill or the source is not JavaScript.

Installation: Install via npm i magic-string for Node.js; browser via magic-string.umd.js script tag; supports module systems, depends on vlq.

Usage: Usage centers on creating a MagicString instance and applying chained edits like update prepend and append while indices always refer to the original string. You can pass options such as filename and offset at construction and finally emit output and a version 3 sourcemap to disk.

Properties: The Properties section documents instance state that tunes how later edits are interpreted. It currently introduces the offset adjustment feature detailed in its subsection.

s.offset: The s.offset property shifts how incoming indices are interpreted for slice update overwrite move remove and left-right insertion methods. For example setting offset to six on hello world makes a bare slice return world.

Methods: The Methods section catalogs the full editing and introspection API for MagicString instances. Most editing methods are chainable and consistently operate on original string indices.

s.addSourcemapLocation(index): This method explicitly registers an original-string index to be included in sourcemap mappings. It only has effect when low resolution mappings are used rather than high resolution mode.

s.append(content): This method adds the given content to the very end of the generated string. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.appendLeft(index, content): This method inserts content at the specified original index with move-aware behavior tied to ranges ending at that index. It returns this and pairs with prependLeft for ordering control at the same position.

s.appendRight(index, content): This method inserts content at the specified original index with move-aware behavior tied to ranges starting at that index. It returns this and pairs with prependRight for ordering control at the same position.

s.clone(): This method creates an independent copy of the MagicString instance with the same current state. It allows speculative or immutable-style workflows without affecting the original.

s.generateDecodedMap(options): This method produces a sourcemap object with raw array-form mappings instead of an encoded mappings string. It accepts the same options as generateMap and is useful when further map manipulation is needed.

s.generateMap(options): This method generates a version 3 sourcemap with optional file source includeContent and hires settings including word-boundary mode. The returned map carries convenient non-enumerable toString and toUrl helpers for serialization and inline DataURI use.

s.hasChanged(): This method reports whether any edits have changed the string from its original value. It provides a quick dirty check before emitting output.

s.indent(prefix[, options]): This method prefixes each line with the given string or with auto-detected indentation defaulting to a tab. It accepts an exclude list of start-end ranges such as multiline strings and returns this.

s.insertLeft(index, content): This method is deprecated since version 0-17 in favor of appendLeft. It remains only for backward compatibility and should not be used in new code.

s.insertRight(index, content): This method is deprecated since version 0-17 in favor of prependRight. It remains only for backward compatibility and should not be used in new code.

s.isEmpty(): This method returns true when the generated source contains only whitespace or nothing at all. It is useful for skipping empty outputs after edits.

s.locate(index): This method is deprecated since version 0-10 and documented via linked pull request 30. It should no longer be used in new code.

s.locateOrigin(index): This method is deprecated since version 0-10 and documented via linked pull request 30. It should no longer be used in new code.

s.move(start, end, index): This method relocates the characters between start and end to the target index in the generated output. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.overwrite(start, end, content[, options]): This method replaces the range from start to end with new content including any appended or prepended inserts in that range. It supports optional storeName for sourcemap names and contentOnly to preserve edge inserts and returns this.

s.prepend(content): This method adds the given content to the very beginning of the generated string. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.prependLeft(index, content): This method behaves like appendLeft but places its content before any prior inserts at the same index. It enables precise ordering control for multiple inserts at one position.

s.prependRight(index, content): This method behaves like appendRight but places its content before any prior inserts at the same index. It enables precise ordering control for multiple inserts at one position.

s.replace(regexpOrString, substitution): This method performs string replacement against the original string using a string or regular expression with string or function substitution. Unlike native replace it always matches the original and mutates state so clone for immutability and returns this.

s.replaceAll(regexpOrString, substitution): This method mirrors replace but replaces all matches instead of just the first one. It requires the global flag when given a regular expression and otherwise follows native replaceAll behavior while returning this.

s.remove(start, end): This method deletes characters from start to end as measured in the original string rather than the generated string. Overlapping or duplicate removals cause an error and it returns this.

s.reset(start, end): This method restores the original characters for the range from start to end and discards prior edits there. It can undo removals and unwanted changes within that span.

s.slice(start, end): This method returns the current generated content corresponding to the original range from start to end. It throws if the referenced characters were already removed.

s.snip(start, end): This method returns a clone containing only the content between start and end of the original string. It discards everything outside that window while preserving edits inside.

s.toString(): This method returns the final generated string after all edits. It is the primary way to read out the transformed result.

s.trim([charType]): This method removes matching characters defaulting to whitespace from both the start and end of the output. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.trimStart([charType]): This method removes matching characters defaulting to whitespace from the start of the output only. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.trimEnd([charType]): This method removes matching characters defaulting to whitespace from the end of the output only. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.trimLines(): This method strips empty lines from the start and end of the output. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.update(start, end, content[, options]): This method replaces the range from start to end with new content while preserving edge inserts unless overwrite is enabled. It supports storeName for sourcemap names and is equivalent to overwrite with contentOnly true and returns this.

Bundling: Bundling concatenates multiple MagicString sources via MagicString Bundle with per-source filename ignoreList and indent exclusion support. The bundle itself supports indent prepend append and map generation with file includeContent and hires options for unified output.

License: The project is released under the MIT license. This permits broad reuse with minimal restriction for council-approved adoption.

Recommendation: Recommend approval for lightweight string transformation with accurate sourcemaps where full AST rewriting is unnecessary, given its small chainable API, hires map support, bundle capability, and permissive MIT licensing with trivial install.",

{"memo":"magic-string: Magic-string is a small fast utility for light string edits with sourcemap generation where full AST rewriting would be overkill. It is intended for non-JavaScript sources as well as JavaScript where comments and formatting must be preserved.

Installation: Install via npm i magic-string for Node; load magic-string.umd.js via script tag for browsers; supports module systems, depends on vlq.

Usage: Usage centers on creating a MagicString instance then applying chainable edits whose indices always refer to the original string. It also shows passing construction options and generating plus writing out version three sourcemaps.

Properties: The Properties section groups instance state that influences later operations rather than performing edits itself. It currently documents only the adjustable offset used to shift positional lookups.

s.offset: The offset property shifts how all position-based APIs interpret incoming indices for slicing and editing. Setting it allows working with a subsection such as a later word while still using original coordinates.

Methods: The Methods section catalogs the full editing and inspection API for MagicString instances. Each entry describes its arguments plus its effect on content or sourcemaps and whether it returns this for chaining.

s.addSourcemapLocation( index ): This method registers an original character index for inclusion in sourcemap mappings when high-resolution output is disabled. It gives fine-grained location control without enabling full high-resolution mode.

s.append( content ): This method adds given content to the end of the generated string. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.appendLeft( index, content ): This method inserts content at a given original index with move-aware behavior tied to ranges ending at that index. It returns this and pairs with prependLeft for ordering control at the same position.

s.appendRight( index, content ): This method inserts content at a given original index with move-aware behavior tied to ranges starting at that index. It returns this and pairs with prependRight for ordering control at the same position.

s.clone(): This method creates an independent copy that preserves current content and editing state. It allows branching or experimental edits without mutating the original instance.

s.generateDecodedMap( options ): This method produces a sourcemap object with raw array-form mappings rather than an encoded string. It is useful when further map manipulation is needed while most users should prefer the encoded generator.

s.generateMap( options ): This method generates a version three sourcemap with optional file name plus source name plus content inclusion plus resolution control. The returned map carries convenience helpers to serialize to JSON or to a data URI for inline use.

s.hasChanged(): This method reports whether the managed string has been modified from its original value. It provides a quick dirty check before further processing or output.

s.indent( prefix[, options] ): This method prefixes each line with a given string or with guessed indentation defaulting to a tab when omitted. It supports an exclusion option for ranges such as multiline strings and returns this for chaining.

s.insertLeft( index, content ): This method is deprecated since version zero point seventeen and should no longer be used. Callers should use appendLeft instead for identical placement behavior.

s.insertRight( index, content ): This method is deprecated since version zero point seventeen and should no longer be used. Callers should use prependRight instead for identical placement behavior.

s.isEmpty(): This method returns true when the resulting source contains only whitespace or nothing at all. It offers a simple emptiness test that ignores formatting characters.

s.locate( index ): This method is deprecated since version zero point ten and points readers to the linked pull request for context. It should not be used in new code.

s.locateOrigin( index ): This method is deprecated since version zero point ten and points readers to the linked pull request for context. It should not be used in new code.

s.move( start, end, index ): This method relocates characters from a start to end range to a new index in the generated output. It returns this to allow chaining with other string operations.

s.overwrite( start, end, content[, options] ): This method replaces the range from start to end with new content including any previously appended or prepended inserts unless configured otherwise. It accepts optional flags for storing original names for sourcemaps and for limiting replacement to content only.

s.prepend( content ): This method inserts given content at the very beginning of the string. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.prependLeft( index, content ): This method behaves like appendLeft except its content is placed before any prior inserts at the same index. It returns this and enables precise ordering of multiple inserts.

s.prependRight( index, content ): This method behaves like appendRight except its content is placed before any prior inserts at the same index. It returns this and enables precise ordering of multiple inserts.

s.replace( regexpOrString, substitution ): This method performs string replacement against the original string using a string or regular expression with string or function substitution. It mutates the instance state rather than returning a new string so callers should clone first for immutable behavior.

s.replaceAll( regexpOrString, substitution ): This method matches the behavior of replace but replaces every match instead of only the first one. It requires a global flag when given a regular expression and returns this for chaining.

s.remove( start, end ): This method deletes characters between start and end as measured in the original string rather than the generated string. It rejects duplicate or partially overlapping removals with an error and returns this.

s.reset( start, end ): This method restores characters between start and end in the original coordinates and discards prior changes in that span. It can undo removals and unwanted edits in the selected interval.

s.slice( start, end ): This method returns generated-string content that corresponds to the slice between start and end in the original string. It throws if the requested indices refer to already removed characters.

s.snip( start, end ): This method returns a clone with all content outside the start to end original range removed. It isolates a substring while preserving editing capabilities in the new instance.

s.toString(): This method returns the current generated string after all applied edits. It provides the final output for writing to disk or further use.

s.trim([ charType ]): This method removes matching characters defaulting to whitespace from both the start and the end. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.trimStart([ charType ]): This method removes matching characters defaulting to whitespace from the start only. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.trimEnd([ charType ]): This method removes matching characters defaulting to whitespace from the end only. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.trimLines(): This method removes empty lines from both the start and the end of the content. It returns this to allow chaining with other edits.

s.update( start, end, content[, options] ): This method replaces the range from start to end with new content while preserving appended or prepended inserts unless the overwrite flag is set. It supports storing original names for sourcemaps and is equivalent to overwrite with content-only mode.

Bundling: Bundling explains how to concatenate multiple MagicString sources with filenames and optional ignore-listing plus indentation handling using the Bundle class. It also covers map generation for the combined output and a shorthand for adding sources that already carry their own metadata.

License: The License section declares that the project is released under the MIT license. It signals permissive reuse with minimal restriction for council approval.

Recommendation: Recommend approval for lightweight string editing with sourcemaps given small fast focused API, chainable edits preserving formatting, Bundle support and permissive MIT licensing, with guidance to use current append and prepend APIs and avoid deprecated locate and insert APIs and to pin versions.","concerns":[],"rationale":"Assembled memo in README document order using Worker 1 for Installation and Worker 2 for all other sections, preserving each as one paragraph, then added closing recommendation to satisfy orchestrator brief for full coverage."}

{"memo": "magic-string: Suppose you have source code that needs light edits like replacing characters or adding a header and footer plus a sourcemap without the weight of recast. Magic-string is a small fast utility for manipulating strings and generating sourcemaps even when the source is not JavaScript.

Installation: Install with npm i magic-string for Node.js; in browsers load magic-string.umd.js via script tag. Works with module systems; requires vlq dependency.

Usage: The section demonstrates a Node workflow where a MagicString is updated by original indices and chained with prepend and append before generating a version 3 sourcemap and writing output files. It also documents constructor options for filename and indent exclusion ranges and ignore list and offset that support later bundling.

Properties: This short section introduces instance properties of MagicString. It currently documents only the offset property that influences position handling.

s.offset: This property adjusts incoming positions for slice and update and overwrite and appendLeft and prependLeft and appendRight and prependRight and move and reset and remove. Setting offset to 6 on hello world makes a later slice return world.

Methods: This section catalogs the editing and inspection and sourcemap methods available on a MagicString instance. Most mutating methods return this to enable chaining.

s.addSourcemapLocation( index ): It registers the given original character index for sourcemap mapping. The registration is only used when high resolution output is disabled.

s.append( content ): It appends the specified content to the end of the string. It returns this to support chaining.

s.appendLeft( index, content ): It inserts content at the given original index from the left side. If a range ending with that index is later moved the insert moves with it and the method returns this.

s.appendRight( index, content ): It inserts content at the given original index from the right side. If a range starting with that index is later moved the insert moves with it and the method returns this.

s.clone(): It creates an independent copy of the MagicString instance. Further edits to the clone do not affect the original.

s.generateDecodedMap( options ): It generates a sourcemap object with raw mappings in array form instead of an encoded string. It accepts the same options as generateMap and suits further manipulation, though most users prefer generateMap.

s.generateMap( options ): It generates a version 3 sourcemap with optional file and source and includeContent and hires settings including word boundary segmentation and custom locations from addSourcemapLocation. The returned map includes non-enumerable toString and toUrl helpers where toUrl yields a data URI for a sourceMappingURL comment.

s.hasChanged(): It reports whether the string has been changed. It returns a boolean reflecting any edits.

s.indent( prefix[, options] ): It prefixes each line with the given prefix, guessing indentation from original content or defaulting to a tab when omitted. An options object may provide an exclude list of start and end ranges such as multiline strings, and the method returns this.

s.insertLeft( index, content ): This method is deprecated since version 0.17. Users should use appendLeft instead.

s.insertRight( index, content ): This method is deprecated since version 0.17. Users should use prependRight instead.

s.isEmpty(): It returns true when the resulting source is empty disregarding whitespace. It offers a quick emptiness check after edits.

s.locate( index ): This method is deprecated since version 0.10. The documentation refers readers to pull request 30 for background.

s.locateOrigin( index ): This method is deprecated since version 0.10. The documentation refers readers to pull request 30 for background.

s.move( start, end, index ): It moves the characters from start to end to the position at index. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.overwrite( start, end, content[, options] ): It replaces characters from start to end with new content including any appended or prepended content in that range under the same restrictions as remove and returns this. An optional fourth argument supports storeName for sourcemap names and contentOnly to limit scope, while update is preferred when appended content should be preserved.

s.prepend( content ): It prepends the specified content to the start of the string. It returns this to support chaining.

s.prependLeft ( index, content ): It behaves like appendLeft at the given original index. Its content goes before any previous appends or prepends at that index and it returns this.

s.prependRight ( index, content ): It behaves like appendRight at the given original index. Its content goes before any previous appends or prepends at that index and it returns this.

s.replace( regexpOrString, substitution ): It performs replacement against the original string using a string or regular expression with a string or function substitution and returns this. Unlike native replace it always matches the original and mutates state, so users should clone for immutable behavior.

s.replaceAll( regexpOrString, substitution ): It works like replace but replaces all matches instead of just one and returns this. When given a regular expression it requires the global flag or throws a TypeError, matching the native replaceAll behavior.

s.remove( start, end ): It removes characters from start to end of the original string rather than the generated string and returns this. Removing the same content twice or making partially overlapping removals causes an error.

s.reset( start, end ): It resets characters from start to end of the original string rather than the generated string. It restores previously removed characters and discards unwanted changes.

s.slice( start, end ): It returns generated string content corresponding to the slice between start and end of the original string. It throws an error when the indices refer to removed characters.

s.snip( start, end ): It returns a clone of the instance. All content before start and after end of the original string is removed in the clone.

s.toString(): It returns the generated string. It reflects all edits applied to the original.

s.trim([ charType ]): It trims content matching charType defaulting to whitespace from both start and end. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.trimStart([ charType ]): It trims content matching charType defaulting to whitespace from the start. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.trimEnd([ charType ]): It trims content matching charType defaulting to whitespace from the end. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.trimLines(): It removes empty lines from the start and end. It returns this to allow chaining.

s.update( start, end, content[, options] ): It replaces characters from start to end with new content under the same restrictions as remove and returns this. An optional fourth argument supports storeName for sourcemap names and an overwrite flag defaulting to false, making the call equivalent to overwrite with contentOnly enabled.

Bundling: The section shows how to concatenate sources with MagicString Bundle by adding sources with filename and content and optional ignore list and indent exclusion ranges, then indenting and wrapping with prepend and append. It documents bundle generateMap options and a shorthand that passes a MagicString instance directly when filename was set at construction.

License: The project is released under the MIT license. It permits reuse with minimal restriction.

Installation: Install via `npm i magic-string` for Node.js; for browsers include `magic-string.umd.js` via script tag. Supports module systems; depends on vlq.

Usage: You create a MagicString instance from source text and apply chainable edits such as update plus prepend and append where indices always refer to the original string. You can then emit the transformed string and a version three source map with content inclusion and file metadata, optionally configuring filename plus indent handling plus ignore listing plus offset for later bundling.

Properties: The Properties section documents the offset field which shifts how incoming positions are interpreted for subsequent editing and slicing operations. Setting offset allows code that works on a substring to reuse original indices, as shown by shifting by six to expose the trailing word in a hello world example.

Methods: The Methods section provides a rich chainable editing API for inserting plus overwriting plus moving plus removing plus resetting plus slicing plus snipping plus trimming plus indenting plus replacing with string or pattern and for cloning plus change detection plus string conversion. It also covers source map generation with high resolution and boundary options plus location hints plus deprecated helpers that now point to newer left and right insertion variants.

Bundling: The Bundling section explains how Bundle concatenates multiple MagicString sources with filenames and ignore list flags and indent exclusions into a single output. {"memo": "What is this? This package provides two extensions that add GFM autolink literal support to mdast through mdast-util-from-markdown and mdast-util-to-markdown. Combined with micromark-extension-gfm-autolink-literal, it covers both GitHub's parse-time and transform-time autolinking behaviors.

When to use this. Use this utility when working with mdast via mdast-util-from-markdown and mdast-util-to-markdown to handle GFM autolink literals, combining the from-markdown extension with the micromark extension for parsing. For full GFM support prefer mdast-util-gfm, for simplicity on remark prefer remark-gfm, and when no syntax tree is needed use micromark alone.

Install. The package is ESM-only and requires Node 16 or newer, installed via npm as mdast-util-gfm-autolink-literal. It can also be imported in Deno and browsers directly from esm.sh with or without bundling.

Use. Usage wires gfmAutolinkLiteral from micromark with gfmAutolinkLiteralFromMarkdown in fromMarkdown to parse www, http/https, and email literals into link nodes. The resulting tree can then be serialized with toMarkdown using gfmAutolinkLiteralToMarkdown, which normalizes www links and others to autolink forms.

API. The package exports two named identifiers, gfmAutolinkLiteralFromMarkdown and gfmAutolinkLiteralToMarkdown, with no default export. Each creates the corresponding mdast extension for handling GFM autolink literals in from-markdown and to-markdown.

gfmAutolinkLiteralFromMarkdown(). This function creates a FromMarkdownExtension that enables parsing of GFM autolink literals into mdast link nodes. It is intended for the mdastExtensions option of mdast-util-from-markdown alongside the micromark extension.

gfmAutolinkLiteralToMarkdown(). This function creates a ToMarkdownExtension that enables serializing mdast link nodes as GFM autolink literals. It is intended for the extensions option of mdast-util-to-markdown.

HTML. This utility does not handle conversion of markdown to HTML itself. That transformation is done by mdast-util-to-hast.

Syntax. The literal syntax is not defined in this package itself. It is documented in the Syntax section of micromark-extension-gfm-autolink-literal.

Syntax tree. This utility adds no new interfaces to mdast. Autolink literals reuse the existing Link interface.

Types. The package is fully typed with TypeScript and exports no additional custom types. Consumers can use the Link type for mdast nodes exposed from @types/mdast.

Compatibility. Projects maintained by the unified collective track maintained versions of Node, with the current 2.x line remaining compatible with Node 16. This utility works with mdast-util-from-markdown version 2 and later and mdast-util-to-markdown version 2 and later.

Related. Related packages include remark-gfm for remark support, mdast-util-gfm for all of GFM, and micromark-extension-gfm-autolink-literal for low-level parsing. Together they place this utility as the autolink-literal slice of the broader GFM ecosystem.

Contribute. Contribution guidance lives in contributing.md in syntax-tree/.github, with help channels described in support.md. Participation is governed by the project code of conduct that all interactions must follow.

License. The project is licensed under MIT. Copyright is held by Titus Wormer.

Recommendation. Adopt mdast-util-gfm-autolink-literal when precise, standards-aligned GFM autolink-literal handling in mdast parsing and serialization is required; prefer mdast-util-gfm or remark-gfm when full GFM support or simplified remark integration is needed, otherwise this focused package provides a stable, typed, MIT-licensed solution for the council's markdown pipeline.","concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in README document order by placing Worker 1's When to use this between Worker 2's What is this? and Install, preserving Worker 2 wording for all other sections as single paragraphs, and added a closing selection recommendation synthesized from the When/API/Related guidance."}

Install: This package is ESM only and is installed with npm on Node 16 and newer. In Deno and browsers it can be imported from the ESM CDN with a bundle query for browser use.

Use: The example parses a document with www and https and email autolinks into an mdast tree with link nodes using fromMarkdown with the micromark and mdast extensions. It then serializes the tree back to markdown with toMarkdown to show normalized link forms with explicit protocols and bracketed autolinks.

API: This package exports the identifiers gfmAutolinkLiteralFromMarkdown and gfmAutolinkLiteralToMarkdown with no default export. Each factory creates an extension for converting GFM autolink literals between markdown and the syntax tree.

gfmAutolinkLiteralFromMarkdown(): It creates an extension for mdast-util-from-markdown to enable GFM autolink literals when parsing. The return value is a FromMarkdownExtension for use in the mdast extensions option.

Types: This package is fully typed with TypeScript and exports no additional types. The mdast Link type is available from the DefinitelyTyped mdast package for consumers.
